status: A12 stays OPEN and the AUTH-05 row does NOT flip. This slice BUILDS the missing capability — a current-password-authenticated password change — and the revocation mechanism that makes 'signs you out everywhere' true of ACCESS tokens and not only refresh tokens. revocation_mechanism.chosen: SESSION-BOUND ACCESS TOKENS. Every access token now carries `sid`, the id of the sessions row it was minted from, and the auth middleware resolves that session on each authenticated request (GetActiveSessionForAccessToken).
revocation_mechanism.cost: ONE indexed read per authenticated request: a primary-key lookup on sessions joined to users by primary key. No in-process cache — vidra runs multiple replicas, so a cache on one process could not be invalidated by a revocation served by another, and immediate invalidation is the whole property being bought.
revocation_mechanism.coverage: The one query covers four revocation sources at once because it re-reads the ACCOUNT rather than trusting the token's copy of it: session revoked, session expired, account deactivated (is_active), account tombstoned (deleted_at).
revocation_mechanism.fail_closed: An access token with no `sid` is refused. Only the previous binary could mint one; its holder's refresh token is untouched, so clients re-authenticate transparently on the next 401. That is the ONE upgrade-visible behaviour of this slice.
revocation_mechanism.also_applied_to: optionalAuth (a revoked or tombstoned principal must not be a principal on identity-varying public routes either) and the private-media access cookie, which mirrors an access token.
revocation_mechanism.rejected: A per-user token_version or sessions_revoked_at column needs a migration and a users-table change for no extra coverage, and sessions_revoked_at additionally has a one-second `iat` race. Neither was adopted.
revocation_mechanism.not_adopted_here: The session lookup could return the account's CURRENT role, making a role demotion effective immediately instead of at token expiry. Left out to keep the diff to the revocation question; recorded as a follow-up.

shipped_rules_as_shipped.endpoint: POST /api/v1/auth/me/password {current_password, new_password} -> 204. Behind requireAuth AND the strict auth limiter.
shipped_rules_as_shipped.wrong_current_password: 403 'incorrect password', nothing changed — the stored hash is byte-identical afterwards, and the caller is not signed out.
shipped_rules_as_shipped.password_policy: The same one registration and the reset enforce (8..72 characters), plus a refusal when the new password equals the current one — a no-op change would still sign out every other device and mail a security notice.
shipped_rules_as_shipped.passwordless_accounts: An account with an EMPTY stored hash (the OAuth/ATProto-only shape) is refused 409 with 'this account has no password: use the password reset flow to set one'. It is deliberately NOT the unfalsifiable 403 it would otherwise get, since bcrypt can never verify an empty hash and no supplied password could ever satisfy it. The UI renders that as a sentence with a real link to /reset-password.
shipped_rules_as_shipped.what_the_change_revokes: Every OTHER session. The caller's own session continues, and its refresh token is deliberately NOT rotated: it is a 256-bit random secret with no relation to the password, and the property that matters — killing whatever an attacker holds — is the revocation of the other sessions.
shipped_rules_as_shipped.notice: A best-effort 'your password was changed' email through the existing mailer seam (SendPasswordChanged, the new sibling of SendPasswordReset). It carries no token, no password and no actionable link. A mailer failure NEVER fails the change.
shipped_rules_as_shipped.no_in_app_notification: There is no in-app notification convention for security events to use: internal/notification's vocabulary is follow / comment / comment_reply / message / report_resolved / video_rejected / caption_ready / new_video / new_report, none of them account-security shaped. The notice is email-only, and adding a type is a product decision plus a prefs-registry row.
shipped_rules_as_shipped.audit: auth.password.change, success and failure (invalid_password, password_not_set). Neither password appears in the event, the response, or any log.

SC1_endpoint.assertions: 30 in the SC1/SC4 driver plus 6 in the rate-limiter driver, 0 failed
SC1_endpoint.authentication: anonymous = 401. Bob supplying ALICE's password = 403 and neither hash moves: the route takes no id, so there is no actor to aim it at.
SC1_endpoint.re_verification: A wrong current password is 403 and the stored hash is byte-identical afterwards; the 403 body echoes neither the supplied password nor the proposed one.
SC1_endpoint.validation: 422 for a missing current_password, a missing new_password, a new password under 8 characters, one over 72, and one identical to the current — and no rejected body moved the hash.
SC1_endpoint.success: 204; the stored value is a fresh bcrypt hash (not the plaintext); the OLD password is then 401 at login and the new one 200.
SC1_endpoint.passwordless: 409 with the reset-flow guidance, and the empty hash is still empty afterwards.
SC1_endpoint.rate_limit: PROVEN on the route itself: an unpaced burst of 14 wrong-password attempts answers 403 nine times and then 429 — the shipped 10/min per-IP auth limiter, never raised for this run. The limiter runs BEFORE requireAuth, so an unauthenticated attacker cannot bypass it. Nothing changed during the burst (asserted from the database, because login shares the same per-IP budget). A general-limiter-only route was unaffected.

SC2_revocation.other_sessions: Alice held three live sessions. A change made from the second one killed the other two on EVERY probed route — GET /auth/me, PATCH /auth/me, GET /me/playlists, POST /playlists, POST /channels, POST /me/export, GET /me/notifications, GET /me/conversations — all 401, measured 0.64s after the change. Exactly ONE un-revoked session row survives. The other session's refresh token is 401 too.
SC2_revocation.current_session: The changer's own access token still reads AND writes (PATCH /auth/me 200), and its refresh token still rotates.
SC2_revocation.deleted_account_reproduction: The deletion slice proved a hard-deleted account creating a channel, a playlist and a fresh archive of ITSELF after its own tombstone. Re-run on this binary: all eight routes 401, and the database confirms the deleted account created no channel, no playlist and no account_exports row.
SC2_revocation.deactivated_account: Same eight routes, all 401 — PATCH /auth/me was 200 before this slice — and the deactivated account's display_name is still empty.
SC2_revocation.admin_disabled_account: An admin flipping is_active to false through PATCH /admin/users/{id} reaches the account's access token too: all five probed routes 401 and nothing was created. Re-enabling does NOT resurrect the old token (the admin path also revokes the sessions) — the user signs in again, and the fresh token works. Recorded as the shipped behaviour.
SC2_revocation.no_session_write_needed: The tagged real-PostgreSQL test proves the strongest form: DeactivateUser writes NO session row at all, and the surviving session immediately stops resolving. The check re-reads the account rather than trusting a revocation having been recorded.
SC2_revocation.browser: See browser_walkthrough — a second browser context is signed out on its next hard reload, 2.5s after the change, while the changer's own context survives a hard reload signed in.

signed_out_device_retry_signed_the_chang.found_by: the acceptance lab, not by reading — the SC2 driver asserted the changer's own session survives and it did not
signed_out_device_retry_signed_the_chang.red_first: "the changer's refresh still works: got 401, want 200" and "exactly one un-revoked session row survives the change: got 0, want 1"
signed_out_device_retry_signed_the_chang.mechanism: Refresh-token REUSE detection assumed compromise and revoked EVERY session whenever a revoked refresh token was presented. That is correct for a replayed ROTATED token, and wrong for a device that was deliberately signed out and whose client simply retried on its first 401 — which is what every client does the moment a password change signs it out. The escalation then took down the very session the change was supposed to keep: the browser the password had just been changed in.
signed_out_device_retry_signed_the_chang.fix: Migration 0128 (append-only) adds sessions.revoked_reason. Rotation stamps 'rotated'; every deliberate sign-out (logout, sign-out-everywhere, a password change, deactivation, the section 1 delete) stamps 'signed_out'. Only a replayed 'rotated' token still escalates. Rows revoked before 0128 carry '' and keep escalating exactly as before, which is the safe direction.
signed_out_device_retry_signed_the_chang.not_weakened: A second test pins what must NOT change: replaying a rotated refresh token still revokes every session, including a freshly rotated one and an unrelated second browser. The real-PostgreSQL test asserts both reasons are actually written.

attempts_and_corrections: The FIRST full vitest run reported 18 failures across 12 files — every one of them an unrelated component (Admin*, Chapters, DownloadButton, InstanceBanner, Search, Studio, Suggestion, UpNext) with a 5-21 second duration. It was run while a Go build, a docker image pull and the lab API were competing for the machine. Re-run unloaded: 1 failure (AdminMediaView's 501-item orphan list, timing out at 5s), which passes on its own — 24/24. Load-induced flakiness, not this diff; recorded rather than hidden.

The status-contract guard TestOpenAPIContractDocumentsGateStatuses broke honestly: its probe minted a SESSION-LESS token, which now 401s everywhere, so it observed 'only 1 of 304 operations were observed to 403'. The probe now authenticates as a fixed principal with a live session; the assertion and its coverage floors are unchanged.

tsc, not vitest, caught the change-password test's ApiError stand-in: it took a bare status number while the real class takes an object, and tsc type-checks the instanceof branches against the REAL class. Vitest was green on the wrong shape.

The FIRST SC2 run failed three assertions that turned out to be one real defect (see defects_found_and_fixed) plus two harness errors: playlists is keyed on owner_id, not user_id, and alice's session count was asserted as a fixed 3 when SC1's own logins had already added more.

The admin-disable phase first probed POST /admin/users/{id}/deactivate, which does not exist (404) — so eight assertions 'failed' against an account that had never been disabled, and its writes landed. The route is PATCH /admin/users/{id} with {is_active:false}. The phase now establishes its starting state explicitly (it deletes its own residue first) because that stale channel survived into the next attempt.

An assumption that the admin path writes no session row was simply WRONG — it revokes them — so that assertion is restated, and the 'no session write needed' proof is carried by the real-PostgreSQL test instead, where DeactivateUser is called directly.

The rate-limiter phase's first attempt measured requireAuth rather than the limiter: it used the token stored in state.json, which SC2 had correctly killed by changing the password from another session. It now signs in fresh. Its closing assertion also had to move from a login to a DATABASE read, because login shares the same per-IP auth budget the burst deliberately exhausts.
Playwright's getByLabel('New password') matches 'Confirm new password' too — three fields, four matches. Every label query is now exact.

An unscoped getByRole('status') grabbed the page's FIRST polite live region (a two-factor spinner), so a failed change appeared to show a success state. Every browser assertion is now scoped to the Password card — the same harness trap the previous A12 slice recorded, hit again.

The browser walkthrough is NOT idempotent (it changes its actor's password), and the first re-run silently signed in with a stale credential and asserted against a signed-out page. It now registers a fresh actor per run.

The auth limiter is 10/min per IP and is shared across register, login, the reset endpoints and now the change endpoint, so repeated walkthrough attempts 429 each other. The API drivers use a FILE-BACKED pacer (a per-process one is what 429'd a previous slice mid-run) and the browser run is spaced by hand.
findings_recorded_not_fixed: The session lookup already returns the account's current state, so making a ROLE demotion effective immediately (instead of at token expiry) is now a one-field change. Not taken here, to keep the diff to the revocation question.

There is no in-app notification type for security events, so a password change reaches the user by email only. On an instance with no working SMTP there is no notice at all — which is the same gap the reset flow has, and is worth an explicit product call alongside it.

The auth limiter is keyed per IP and shared across register / login / reset / change. On an instance behind a proxy that does not set a trusted client IP, one user can exhaust everyone's budget. Out of scope here; noted because this slice adds a route to that shared bucket.
Deactivation still enqueues no search event (recorded by the deletion slice and unchanged), and the admin 'Reactivate' control still exists on tombstoned rows. Neither is touched by this slice.

for_the_next_slice.what_remains_for_AUTH_05_to_flip: EMAIL change with re-verification, and nothing else. Profile/privacy and the account archive were closed by the profile slice; deactivation, deletion with content, the search deletion hook, DM retention and media cleanup by the deletion slice; and password change with re-verification is closed here, on a mechanism whose revocation now reaches access tokens. The register row's remaining clause describes a capability vidra still does not ship: an account's address is fixed at registration, PATCH /auth/me rejects an `email` field with 422, and even the instance owner cannot move one (PATCH /admin/users/{id} 422s an email and can only toggle email_verified) — all proven by 12 route probes in the profile slice.
what_the_email_slice_should_know: The re-verification shape is settled: mirror this endpoint's request shape and error semantics (current password re-verified, 403 for wrong, 409 for a password-less account, the same auth limiter group). An email change needs BOTH the current password AND possession of the NEW address, so it is a two-step flow — a pending_email column plus a confirmation token — not a PATCH.

Revocation is no longer a question. Access tokens are session-bound, so whatever an email change decides to revoke actually bites within one request. Deciding whether it SHOULD revoke is the product call.

The mailer seam now has three senders (SendPasswordReset, SendPasswordChanged, SendEmailVerification) and one obvious fourth: a notice to the OLD address that the account's email was changed, which is the only signal that reaches a user whose address was stolen. Do not skip it.

users.email is NOT NULL with a unique index, and login resolves email-or-username with EMAIL TAKING PRECEDENCE (usernames may look like emails). An email change must therefore not create an address that collides with anybody's username-shaped login, and the '@'-ban on new usernames is the existing half of that rule.
sessions.revoked_reason (0128) exists now: a deliberate sign-out must stamp 'signed_out', or a signed-out client's retry will escalate to revoking everything — the defect this slice found.
